recorded: 11 April 1950, Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York; LP published 1951
question: How can a lullaby sound both cumbersome and tender?
intro: A low, solitary melody gradually acquires rocking accompaniment and a wider singing range. The score asks for tenderness with a little awkwardness; follow how Debussy preserves both qualities as the lullaby fills out.

sections.label: A · The low lullaby
sections.mNote: a solitary low melody meets sparse, soft replies

sections.label: B · The rocking song
sections.mNote: a fuller accompaniment supports a growing melodic span

sections.label: A′ · Quiet recollection
sections.mNote: the opening melody returns with a softer rocking background

cues.title: Tenderness with an awkward step
cues.text: The low opening line is marked “gentle and a little awkward”. Its pauses and sparse replies matter as much as the melody itself. Listen for the space around each phrase before the accompaniment becomes more continuous.
cues.evidence: Viewed Durand score, printed p. 6: doux et un peu gauche, low unaccompanied melody and sparse upper notes. The report places the first substantial increase in level around 0:50, after the restrained opening. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0d/IMSLP252526-PMLP02387-Debussy%2C_Claude-Childrens_Corner_Durand_7188_filter.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A toy, not a portrait
cues.text: Morris Hastings’s note on this Columbia LP identifies Jimbo as a felt toy elephant. That is a useful image for the low, slightly ungainly melody, but the music does not require us to invent a scene or a particular bedtime in Debussy’s household.
cues.evidence: The original LP sleeve note by Morris Hastings describes Jimbo as a felt toy elephant. This is attributed programme commentary, not independent documentation of a specific event: https://archive.org/download/lp_childrens-corner-suite-forest-scenes-o_claude-debussy-robert-schumann-robert-c_0/lp_childrens-corner-suite-forest-scenes-o_claude-debussy-robert-schumann-robert-c_0_djvu.txt

cues.title: Rocking beneath the song
cues.text: In the fuller middle stretch, separate the longer melodic notes from the repeated movement underneath them. The accompaniment keeps the lullaby rocking while the upper line can linger, rise and fall at its own pace.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp. 7–8 shows the moving lower accompaniment, sustained melodic notes and Un peu plus mouvementé. The report’s 0:50 change and higher levels through 1:05–2:10 support this broad middle passage; the cue does not identify a single entrance at 1:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Session and issue are different
cues.text: Casadesus recorded Children’s Corner in Columbia’s 30th Street Studio, New York, on 11 April 1950. The LP used for this transfer is dated 1951. The recording session and the publication of this particular carrier are separate events.
cues.evidence: The official Casadesus discography names the session date, venue and ML 4366: https://www.robertcasadesus.com/en/discography/. The 1951 LP publication is corroborated by the library catalogue: https://ci.nii.ac.jp/ncid/BB26857496. Neither date is an Internet Archive upload date.

cues.title: The first voice returns
cues.text: As the lullaby withdraws, recognise the low opening melody inside the quieter texture. The return is not quite as bare as the beginning: the rocking motion helps familiar material settle rather than starting the piece afresh.
cues.evidence: Viewed score p. 9 supplies Retenu, 1° Tempo and the returning melody with moving accompaniment. The report’s strongest change is at 2:18, after relative level falls around 2:10–2:20. The boundary is approximate; the report’s machine key labels are not used to identify harmony.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Quiet without dragging
cues.text: The closing page asks for continued softness without slowing, then for the sound to die away. Listen for the difference between diminishing sound and a pulse that simply loses direction.
cues.evidence: Viewed score p. 9 gives Sempre pp et Sans retarder and morendo. The final five-second windows are among the quietest in the 178.1-second file. This compares written instructions with the broad recorded withdrawal; it does not claim a measured beat-by-beat tempo.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A solitary voice gains an accompaniment
transitions.how: The sparse opening gives way to a more continuous exchange between a moving lower line and longer melodic notes above. Debussy preserves the gentle character while filling the gaps with a rocking accompaniment; the later instruction Un peu plus mouvementé allows more movement without turning the lullaby into a march. Texture and phrase length distinguish the new span more clearly than a sharply announced new key.
transitions.evidence: The report marks a strong boundary at 0:50 and a rise from the quiet 0:45 window to sustained higher levels after 0:50. Viewed Durand score pp. 6–8 supplies the sparse opening, moving accompaniment and later tempo instruction. The paragraph describes the surrounding transition, not a single aligned instruction.

transitions.title: The lullaby remembers its opening
transitions.how: After the middle span’s greater range and fuller chords, Debussy holds the motion back and restores the first tempo. The opening melody becomes recognisable again, now supported by the gentle descending movement below it. The return reduces weight rather than making a grand arrival; low repeated notes and diminishing sound carry the same material towards the end.
transitions.evidence: Viewed score p. 9 supplies Retenu, 1° Tempo, the melodic return and dying close. The report places its strongest change at 2:18 and shows a broad reduction after the louder 1:45–2:05 region. This is an approximate passage boundary, not a bar-aligned return.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
French Symbolist poetry · Russian music · Javanese gamelan · eighteenth-century French keyboard music
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
